newsitem.title: POLAND: Law enforcers, firms seek to brake car crime.
newsitem.headline: Law enforcers, firms seek to brake car crime.

text.p: Automakers, insurers and law enforcers from around the world met in Warsaw on Monday to find ways to get tough on car theft, a booming business for international crime gangs costing billions of dollars a year.

The United Nations-sponsored two-day conference, with delegates from 28 countries, is discussing how to fight slick thieves who spirit vehicles across frontiers more easily than official agencies can cooperate to trace and retrieve them.

"The aim is transnational cooperation among governments and law enforcement agencies...so the good guys can cooperate as quickly and efficiently as the bad guys," Jonathan Winer, Deputy Assistant Secretary of the U.S. Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement told Reuters.
Many countries have not treated car theft very seriously, Eduardo Vetere, officer in charge of the crime prevention division of the U.N. office in Vienna, told the conference.
"The problem, however, has radically changed," Vetere said, adding that proceeds from car theft and smuggling were being fed into narcotics and other ugly crime by diversified gangs.
Well-organised international groups were bribing law, customs and insurance company officials, spreading corruption which undermined democracy and development in some countries.
Vetere pointed to a growth in violent hijackings as new immobilisers made traditional methods harder.
"Many citizens have been wounded or killed by criminals who wanted to deprive them of their cars," he said.

Delegates all stress the need for cooperation between government agencies, the experienced sleuths of the insurance industry and manufacturers who stamp identity numbers on vehicles and are evolving ever-better security devices.
They also seek a quick, effective exchange of information between countries and clear procedures for returning vehicles which have been found stolen in other countries.
One measure of the problem is a lack of global statistics -- estimates of the scale of car theft now vary widely.

Elizabeth Good, car crime specialist for Interpol in Geneva, told Reuters that in Europe 1.5 to two million vehicles were stolen a year, of which half were not recovered -- though prevention was now cutting theft in major car-making countries.
Interpol this year launched a centralised computer system to pool countries' databases on car thefts and Good said four, including Russia, were already joined up to it.
"Our message is: Here is a tool for you. It is available now, it is just the question of taking the necessary steps to make it a reality," she said.
Winer said that $6 to $7 billion worth of cars were stolen in the United States annually, a third of which left the country.

Apart from common databases, U.S. delegates were urging greater international standardisation of identification numbers on cars and parts and better procedures for returning vehicles identified as having been stolen in other countries -- modelled on such U.S. treaties with Caribbean and Latin American states.

Such international arrangements for faster recovery are sought by insurers, Cornelia Vallis of the Paris-based Comite Europeen des Assurances said -- especially as insurance firms in Europe often have to pay out 30 days after a car is stolen.

A representative of the German car manufacturers was presenting new technological means including gadgets that will allow a stolen car to be traced electronically, remotely disabled, or that will set a limit on the time or distance a vehicle can go before shutting down.
